interest: This collection is particularly valuable for diplomatic and naval historians tracing how U.S. diplomats and naval intelligence monitored and interpreted Japanese operational war doctrine following the 1930 London Naval Treaty. Most striking is Edwin L. Neville's June 1930 dispatch, which accurately outlines Japan's interceptive attrition strategy (yōgeki sakusen)—using long-range naval aviation and submarines deployed across the Caroline and Marshall Islands to degrade the U.S. Pacific Fleet advancing toward the Philippines. The subsequent documents demonstrate the rapid geographical expansion of Japanese naval exercises between 1930 and 1936, shifting from fleet reviews and domestic propaganda drills to expansive northern operations off the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka, and culminating in southward maneuvers toward the Celebes and Moluccas that stoked regional fears of Japanese expansion into the Dutch East Indies.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.31, spanning June 1930 through May 1936) contains diplomatic despatches, military intelligence reports, official correspondence, and cross-reference sheets documenting the maneuvers and strategic doctrine of the Imperial Japanese Navy. Following the conclusion of the 1930 London Naval Treaty, American observers closely tracked Japanese efforts to compensate for submarine treaty limitations by expanding naval aviation and conducting extensive exercises in the South Seas Mandate (Caroline and Marshall Islands). The file also chronicles diplomatic protocols surrounding the exclusion of foreign warships from the 1930 Grand Naval Review off Kobe, propaganda-oriented army and navy maneuvers in 1933, large-scale 1935 maneuvers in the North Pacific reaching the Kurils and Kamchatka under Vice Admiral Sankichi Takahashi, and 1936 fleet concentrations near the Celebes and Moluccas that heightened Dutch concerns over Japanese southward expansion.

subfiles.about: Transmits a press report on Japanese naval air maneuvers in the Caroline and Marshall Islands and analyzes Japanese naval war strategy against the United States.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville transmits a translated clipping from the Tokyo Jiji Shimpo concerning naval air exercises in the South Seas Mandate and evaluates Japanese naval strategy in the event of war with the United States. He notes that Japanese planners anticipate an immediate transfer of the U.S. fleet to the Philippines, which the Japanese Navy intends to harass and deplete using submarines and long-range aircraft while passing through the Caroline and Marshall Islands. Neville highlights Baron Shidehara's statements in the Diet that reductions in submarine tonnage accepted under the London Naval Treaty would be compensated for by other defensive means, notably the expansion of naval aviation.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 160 from Edwin L. Neville on Japanese Naval Air Manoeuvres in the South Seas

subfiles.about: Reports on the planned long-range flight of the Oppama Air Squadron from Yokosuka to Saipan to participate in joint exercises with the Second Battle Fleet.
subfiles.summary: This translation of an article from the Tokyo Jiji Shimpo details plans for six large seaplanes of the Oppama Air Squadron to fly 1,200 miles from Yokosuka to Saipan on June 14, 1930. The exercise was designed to test operational war conditions under the post-London Naval Conference defense scheme in coordination with thirty-six warships of the Second Battle Fleet already operating off Saipan. The fleet included advanced submarines and four 10,000-ton cruisers—the Ashigara, Haguro, Nachi, and Myoko—scheduled to conclude maneuvers and head north by mid-June.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Jiji Shimpo Article on Extensive Air Manoeuvres in the South Seas

subfiles.about: Forwards a request from the Japanese Ministry of Marine asking American warships to keep clear of Kobe and Osaka during the 1930 Grand Naval Review.
subfiles.summary: The Navy Department transmits to the Secretary of State a translated note received from the U.S. Naval Attaché in Tokyo originating from the Japanese Ministry of Marine. The Japanese communication requested that American naval vessels avoid the waters of Kobe and Osaka during the Grand Naval Review scheduled for October 26, 1930. The letter confirms that instructions in accordance with the Japanese request have been forwarded to the Commander-in-Chief of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet.
subfiles.title: Letter from the Navy Department to the Secretary of State regarding the Japanese Grand Naval Review

subfiles.about: Informs the U.S. Naval Attaché that foreign warships are not invited to the Grand Naval Review off Kobe and requests that American ships avoid the area.
subfiles.from: M. Koga, Aide, Ministry of Marine, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Commander M. Koga notifies U.S. Naval Attaché Captain J. V. Ogan that the Imperial Japanese Navy's Grand Naval Review of 1930 will take place off Kobe on October 26, 1930, without invitations extended to foreign warships. Citing heavy maritime congestion expected in the ports of Osaka and Kobe before and after the event, Koga asks that arrangements be made through the Navy Department and the Commander-in-Chief of the Asiatic Fleet to keep American warships away from the region.
subfiles.title: Note No. 2671 from Japanese Ministry of Marine to Captain J. V. Ogan regarding the 1930 Grand Naval Review
subfiles.to: Captain J. V. Ogan, Naval Attaché, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 510 regarding propaganda maneuvers conducted by the Japanese Army and Navy in August 1933.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file sheet indexes Despatch No. 510 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, dated September 5, 1933, originally filed under 894.00 P.R./69. Grew reports that both the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy staged maneuvers of a propaganda nature during August 1933. The cross-reference records these military exercises under decimal file 894.31 concerning Japanese naval maneuvers.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 510 from Grew on August 1933 Military and Naval Maneuvers

subfiles.about: Transmits a press report from the Paris newspaper Le Temps concerning large-scale Japanese naval maneuvers planned for 1935–1936 in the North Pacific.
subfiles.summary: An Office of Naval Intelligence Attaché's Report forwarding an excerpt from the Paris daily Le Temps regarding the Imperial Japanese Navy's upcoming grand maneuvers for the 1935–1936 fiscal year. Commanded by Vice Admiral Sankichi Takahashi, the exercises received an unprecedented budget allocation of six million yen as the capstone of a three-year defense program. The planned maneuvers involved 192 warships and 200 aircraft, operating off the Japanese home coast before advancing northward toward the Kuril Islands, Kamchatka, and the North Pacific.
subfiles.title: U.S. Naval Attaché Report on Japanese 1935-1936 Grand Naval Maneuvers in the North Pacific
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 433 regarding reports of Japanese fleet maneuvers near the Celebes and Moluccas.
subfiles.from: Walter A. Foote, U.S. Consul at Batavia
subfiles.summary: A State Department document file sheet referencing Despatch No. 433 dated May 11, 1936, filed under decimal file 756d.94/11. Consul Walter A. Foote reports on intelligence leaked from Tokyo, Shanghai, and Swatow indicating that seventy-five Japanese warships under Admiral Sankichi Takahashi were preparing to conduct maneuvers near the Celebes and Moluccas. The dispatch emphasizes that these impending operations heightened fears in the Netherlands East Indies regarding potential Japanese military aggression.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 433 from Foote on Japanese Fleet Maneuvers near the Dutch East Indies
